terms.definition: The on-demand delivery of IT resources (compute, storage, databases, networking) over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing — you pay only for what you use.
terms.example: Instead of buying a server, you rent EC2 compute power from AWS for exactly the hours you need it.

terms.definition: Getting IT resources instantly when needed, without advance ordering or waiting. A core characteristic of cloud computing.
terms.example: Launching an EC2 instance takes under 60 seconds — no procurement process, no waiting for hardware delivery.

terms.definition: A pricing model where you are charged only for actual resource usage, with no upfront commitment. Stop using, stop paying.
terms.example: An EC2 instance running for 5 hours is billed for 5 hours. Terminated? Billing stops.

terms.definition: A cloud service model that provides raw building blocks: compute, storage, and networking. The customer manages OS, runtime, and applications. AWS example: EC2.
terms.example: Renting a plot of land — AWS gives you the land (virtual server), you build the house (OS, software, apps).

terms.definition: A cloud service model where the provider manages the underlying infrastructure (OS, runtime, scaling). The customer only manages application code and data. AWS example: Elastic Beanstalk.
terms.example: A furnished apartment — AWS handles the building and maintenance, you just move in with your app code.

terms.definition: A complete software product delivered over the internet, run and managed entirely by the provider. The customer just uses the software. AWS example: Amazon Rekognition.
terms.example: Gmail, Netflix, Dropbox — you use the app, you manage nothing underneath.

terms.definition: A physical geographic location in the world containing a cluster of AWS data centers, organized into Availability Zones. Most AWS services are scoped to a Region.
terms.example: us-east-1 (N. Virginia), eu-west-1 (Ireland), ap-south-1 (Mumbai) are all AWS Regions.

terms.definition: An isolated data center facility within an AWS Region. Each Region has 3–6 AZs, physically separated to prevent disaster cascades, connected by high-bandwidth private networking.
terms.example: ap-southeast-2a, ap-southeast-2b, ap-southeast-2c are the three AZs in Sydney's AWS Region.

terms.definition: A smaller AWS infrastructure node (400+ globally) that caches and delivers content close to end users for low latency. Used primarily by Amazon CloudFront (CDN).
terms.example: A user in Mumbai watching Netflix gets content from a nearby Edge Location rather than a distant Region.

terms.definition: AWS's framework defining security responsibility boundaries: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud (physical infrastructure); the customer is responsible for security IN the cloud (data, config, access).
terms.example: AWS secures the data center. The customer secures their S3 bucket permissions and EC2 firewall rules.

terms.definition: Upfront investment in physical assets like servers and data centers. Traditional IT model — you own and depreciate the hardware.
terms.example: Spending $500,000 to buy servers for a new data center is CAPEX.

terms.definition: Ongoing usage-based spending. Cloud computing converts CAPEX to OPEX — you pay monthly for what you consume rather than buying hardware upfront.
terms.example: Paying AWS $2,000/month for EC2 and S3 usage is OPEX — no hardware purchase required.

terms.definition: As AWS's customer base grows, AWS can purchase hardware at bulk discounts and operate more efficiently — savings that are passed to customers through lower prices.
terms.example: AWS has passed over 100 price reductions to customers since launch as their scale has grown.

terms.definition: The ability to instantly scale cloud resources up or down based on demand, automatically and without manual intervention.
terms.example: Auto-scaling group grows from 5 EC2 instances to 50 during a Black Friday spike, then shrinks back overnight.

terms.definition: Multiple customers (tenants) sharing the same physical AWS infrastructure, with logical isolation at the hypervisor level preventing cross-customer access.
terms.example: Your EC2 instance and a competitor's EC2 instance may run on the same physical server — completely isolated.

terms.definition: A cloud environment used exclusively by one organization, not shared with the public. Can be managed internally or by a third party like Rackspace.
terms.example: A bank running its own internal cloud infrastructure that no other organization can access.

terms.definition: Cloud infrastructure owned and operated by a third-party provider (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) and delivered over the internet to multiple customers simultaneously.
terms.example: AWS is the world's largest public cloud — anyone with an account can provision resources.

terms.definition: A deployment model mixing on-premises (or private cloud) infrastructure with public cloud, connected securely. Sensitive workloads stay on-premises; flexible workloads use public cloud.
terms.example: A hospital keeps patient records on-premises (compliance) but uses AWS for analytics and backups.

terms.definition: An AWS service that is not scoped to a specific Region — it applies worldwide. IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, and WAF are global services.
terms.example: IAM users and roles created in your account are visible and functional in every AWS Region automatically.

terms.definition: Legal or regulatory requirements that mandate data must remain within a specific geographic jurisdiction. The top factor when selecting an AWS Region.
terms.example: GDPR may require EU citizen data to remain within EU AWS Regions like eu-west-1 (Ireland) or eu-central-1 (Frankfurt).
